name: The First 90 Days
title: The First 90 Days
answer: The First 90 Days is a role-based starting plan for superintendents, principals, teachers, and parents, laid out in Figure 20.5. It turns the Volume's Thirty Day Moves into concrete early actions and requires no new technology purchases. It matters because it gives schools and families a clear place to begin with governance, people, practice, and understanding.

sections.body: The First 90 Days is a starting plan for leaders and families who ask where to begin. Figure 20.5 lays out separate first 90 day lists for a superintendent, a principal, a teacher, and a parent. Each list draws on the Thirty Day Moves found throughout the Volume. None of the lists requires buying new technology. The idea solves the problem of an unclear starting point by giving each role concrete early actions.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text organizes the first 90 days by role, not by grade band. Superintendents publish the approved tool list and the human review rule, model AI use where others can see it, choose one pilot with a clear measure and a comparison group, and report results to the board including what did not work. Principals name an AI champion, run a small time study with volunteers, decide with teachers where saved time will go, check that every AI tool in the building is approved, and share learning with staff and families. Teachers try AI for one planning task and one feedback task, check every output, label assignments with AI use levels, build revision into class time, and keep student names and work out of tools not on the approved list. Parents ask the school the five questions from Chapter 14, talk with their child about AI use and ask them to explain their work, attend a parent AI night if one is offered, and share what they learn with other families.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no evidence label, study, or finding. It presents Figure 20.5 as a planning layout for the first 90 days, not as research. So this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits around approved tools and human review. Every AI output a teacher uses must be checked, and student names and work must stay out of tools not on the approved list. Principals must confirm that every AI tool in the building is approved, and they decide with teachers where saved time will go. Superintendents must report results to the board, including what did not work, so the pilot remains accountable. The choices about review, tool approval, time use, and family conversations stay with people, and parents keep the decision to talk with their child and ask for explanations of work.
